transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 14:00 ET - Duration 42m
Attendees: Alex Harper (Redwood AE), Sanjay Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Head of AI, Zephyr), Raj Singh (Platform Lead, Zephyr), Lina Ortiz (CISO, Zephyr)

00:00 Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate it. I'm Alex, AE on the account, with Sanjay from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Maya (Zephyr): Hi Alex, good thanks. Excited to dig in, we've been evaluating a couple options.
00:10 Raj (Zephyr): Morning - excuse me, afternoon, yeah - we'll try to keep it focused, got a couple specific questions on Dedicated.
00:18 Alex: Perfect. Quick agenda - 1) your current infra + constraints, 2) Redwood Dedicated overview and how we handle reserved GPUs, burst and scaling, 3) security/compliance fit, and 4) next steps. Sound good?
00:28 Maya: Yep.
00:30 Sanjay (Redwood SE): I'll lean into the sizing and performance bits, and we can go deeper if you want.
00:34 Lina (Zephyr CISO): I'll probably jump in on the security bits.
00:36 Alex: Great. Raj, want to kick off with current stack and what you're trying to solve?
00:40 Raj: Sure. We're running a mix of cloud VMs and some on-prem infra for sensitive workloads. Currently doing some in-house hosting of models for chat and fraud detection - latency is okay but costs are creeping up. We need predictable throughput for peak trading windows and strict network isolation for regulated datasets.
00:55 Maya: And we have a roadmap to expand models - embeddings, reranking, and a few LLM assistants, so scale will grow quickly.
01:02 Sanjay: Got it. When you say predictable throughput for peaks, can you share target QPS and peak concurrency?
01:08 Maya: Ballpark - 120 requests/sec for embeddings during batch jobs, and about 30 concurrent realtime chat sessions, peaks up to 100 concurrent tokens/sec across models during end-of-day runs.
01:20 Sanjay: Useful, thanks. That maps to reserved GPU sizing - we typically recommend N GPUs for base commit and then burst pool for short windows.
01:27 Alex: Quick note on terminology - Dedicated equals reserved capacity with isolation, you can pin model versions; Private is the VPC/on-prem control plane option.
01:35 Raj: We're leaning Dedicated with VPC peering for now, maybe Private later. Main ask is: how does your burst strategy work? We can't overprovision for rare spikes.
01:44 Sanjay: We support a configurable burst pool; essentially you commit base capacity (reserved GPUs) and then enable burst capacity which can use spare capacity within your Dedicated pool or cross-tenant spare depending on your contract. For strict isolation contracts we enable burst from a contracted burst bucket - there are tradeoffs with cost and SLOs.
02:02 Maya: When you say "spare capacity" do you mean other customers' machines? That's a hard no for some of our regulatory models.
02:09 Sanjay: Understood - for contracts needing strict isolation we offer fully isolated burst within your reserved machines or a pre-allocated burst buffer. So you don't share hardware with other tenants during burst. That option is higher cost but keeps the isolation property.
02:21 Lina: We need that in writing - audit logs, and demonstrable no co-tenancy for the regulated datasets. Also KMS integration for key management and HSM compatibility are requirements.
02:30 Alex: Absolutely. We can include non-co tenancy language in the Dedicated SOW and show KMS/HSM integration docs. We support customer-managed keys and key wrapping via your KMS, and audit logs through Redwood Console.
02:40 Raj: What about autoscaling? We have variable load; we'd like elastic growth but predictability.
02:46 Sanjay: You can do policy-based autoscaling - scale by queue depth, GPU utilization, or request latency. For Dedicated we recommend setting a base commit to cover steady-state and an autoscale window that triggers burst to pre-provisioned capacity. Autoscale to cloud+burst can be configured for either hot-warm tiers.
03:05 Maya: Any impact to latency when scaling up? We can't tolerate a 5-10s cold-start for chat.
03:11 Sanjay: We use continuous batching plus prewarmed cache nodes. For chat flows that need low tail latency we recommend keeping a small pool of warm replicas and using prefix/KV cache. That keeps cold-starts to sub-second for most models. There are some edge cases for very large context models where warming takes longer.
03:28 Raj: On the model side we will probably quantize some models - do you support INT8 or related kernels?
03:34 Sanjay: Yes - runtime supports quantized execution paths and we can recommend quantization profiles per model. We also provide recommended kernels and can run a benchmark pass during pilot.
03:43 Maya: Speaking of benchmarks - we need to validate cost per token and latency against our workloads. Can you run benchmarks using our prompt sets?
03:49 Sanjay: Totally. For pilots we run your workload against candidate GPU flavors (A10G, H100 equivalents) and provide a benchmark sheet. We'll include token throughput, p95 latency, and cost estimates including batching effects.
03:59 Alex: We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and suggested GPU configs as part of the follow up.
04:04 Lina: For security - SOC2 reports, penetration test results, and an architecture diagram are needed. Also SSO/SAML and RBAC for admin roles.
04:14 Alex: We have SOC2 Type II report, can share the redacted report and pen test summary; SAML and SCIM for provisioning and RBAC are supported in Redwood Console. Audit logs are retained per your retention policy; we can discuss retention windows.
04:27 Raj: Network setup - VPC peering vs private link? Which is better for lower egress and simpler routing?
04:33 Sanjay: VPC peering is simpler for most customers; PrivateLink gives you more control over endpoints and reduces surface area but has additional config. For low latency we often recommend peering in the same region.
04:44 Maya: Pricing question - how is dedicated priced? Flat monthly per-GPU plus usage?
04:49 Alex: Standard model is a committed monthly GPU fee for reserved capacity and per-token or per-inference usage for burst beyond your commit, or a flat burst buffer pricing depending on contract. We can propose a few options in the pricing deck.
04:59 Raj: And SLAs for latency/uptime?
05:02 Alex: SLA tiers are in the Dedicated contract; uptime SLAs and latency SLOs for reserved pools can be included with enterprise add-ons. We'll include typical SLA numbers in the deck.
05:12 Maya: One more - data residency. Some of our data must stay in-region.
05:16 Alex: We support region pinning for Dedicated and Private deployments; we'll note region availability.
05:20 Raj: Any known gotchas? For example, model split across GPUs and KV cache consistency?
05:25 Sanjay: For larger models we shard and maintain KV cache consistency with our runtime; there's tuning required for cross-GPU attention. We'll handle that as part of model onboarding. Also, prompt prefix caching helps reduce cost for repeated prompts.
05:38 Lina: What's the onboarding timeline from contract to pilot?
05:42 Alex: Typical is 4-6 weeks: contract and SOW, infra provisioning and network setup (1-2 weeks), model onboarding + benchmarks (2-3 weeks), pilot run. Faster timelines possible with template SOW.
05:56 Maya: That's reasonable.
05:58 Alex: Any other questions?
06:00 Raj: Just one - can we get a test tenant for smoke tests?
06:04 Alex: Yes, we can provision a sandbox Dedicated pilot environment. We'll include that in the pilot proposal.
06:09 Sanjay: We'll also capture the QPS and sample workloads so benchmarking is realistic.
06:12 Maya: Okay great.
06:14 Lina: We'll send the security questionnaire and list of compliance items internally by next week.
06:18 Alex: Awesome. Quick recap - Alex will send pricing/SLA and SOW template, Sanjay will send benchmark sheet and GPU recommendations, Maya will provide sample prompts and workloads, Lina will circulate security questionnaire. Follow-up deep-dive with infra team week of 3/16.
06:34 Maya: Thanks everyone.
06:36 Alex: Thanks. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
06:40 (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains transcription artifacts; names and acronyms sometimes abbreviated. References to product names: Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPUs), Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem), Redwood Console (observability).
